(p-105) Surat al-Mu'minun (The Believers)

Its purpose is to single out the believers for success. Its name is clearly indicative of this. ﴿In the name of God﴾, to whom belongs all command, so none can reverse His command. ﴿The Most Merciful﴾, whose universal mercy includes making things clear in explanation. ﴿The Most Compassionate﴾, who singled out whomever He willed for faith.

When the previous surah was concluded with the call to "those who believe" and their being commanded in matters of religion, both specific and general, and when it ended with prayer, zakat, and being protected by Him (glorified is He), described by what was mentioned, this led those addressed to expect every good. So this surah begins with what produces seeking refuge in Him (glorified is He) in prayer and other aspects of religion in both abodes. God, exalted, opens with the particle of expectation ﴿qad﴾ (indeed), which is the opposite of what it affirms as expected, brings the past closer to the present, and negates what it denies. ﴿Has succeeded﴾, meaning has won, prevailed, and attained now everything he desires, and obtained lasting permanence in good. ﴿The believers﴾. He used the noun form to indicate that whoever affirms faith and acts on what he was commanded in the end of the previous surah deserves the established attribute, because he has been mindful of God, spent from what he was provided, and so has succeeded. ﴿And whoever is protected from the stinginess of his own soul, those are the successful﴾.

Then He qualified them with what necessarily follows from sincerity in faith, saying: ﴿those who﴾, i.e., with their inner selves and their outward conduct, ﴿in their prayer﴾. [The prayer] is attributed to them to encourage them to preserve it, because it lies between them and Allah the Exalted, and He is free of need of it, so they are the ones who benefit from it. ﴿Humbly submissive﴾ (khushu', i.e., lowly, still, humble, tranquil), with their inner and outer selves confined to what they are engaged in. Al-Razi said: "Fearful, with a fear that fills the heart with reverence, refines the character, and disciplines the limbs," i.e., out of fear that their prayer might be rejected. Among this is lowering the gaze to the place of prostration. Al-Razi said: "When the servant enters the prayer, he lifts the veil, and when he turns, he lowers it." He said: "This is a fear mixed with vigilance and humility. It may also appear in dealings as preference, courtesy, fairness and moderation, and in service as presence and submissiveness, and in secret as veneration, modesty and reverence." Khushu' in prayer is by gathering one's resolve upon it and turning away from everything else, which is achieved through presence of heart, understanding, veneration, awe, hope and shame. If this is their state in the prayer, which is the nearest of the acts of drawing near to Allah, then they are more deserving of it in other than it.

Ibn Kathir said: "Khushu' in prayer is only attained by one who empties his heart for it, occupies himself with it to the exclusion of other things, and prefers it over others. Then it becomes a rest for him and a coolness of the eyes," as in the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "The coolness of my eyes has been placed in prayer," narrated by Ahmad and al-Nasa'i from Anas (may Allah be pleased with him). And [the Prophet (ﷺ)] said: "O Bilal! Give us rest with the prayer," narrated by Ahmad from a man of Aslam (may Allah be pleased with him).

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 23, verse 3:

(p-107) Since both the prayer and the humility (khushu') act as a barrier against idle talk (laghw), he followed it with His saying: ﴿And those who turn away﴾ with their inner selves, which their outward conduct follows, ﴿from idle talk﴾, that is, what does not concern them, and it is everything that deserves to be dropped and discarded, ﴿turning away﴾, that is, deliberately abandoning it. Thus they combine doing what concerns them with leaving aside what does not concern them.

Having joined the two foundations of the building of obligations, namely performing khushu' (humble submissiveness) and abandoning idle talk (laghw), and since man is a locus of weakness and a center of shortcoming, such that he scarcely remains free of what does not concern him, and since wealth expiates what is intended of faith, let alone what is mentioned of it by way of idle talk, wealth therefore expiates idle talk outside of oaths a fortiori, ﴿Take from their wealth a charity by which you purify them and cleanse them﴾ [al-Tawbah: 103]. He followed this with His saying: ﴿And those who﴾, and he affirmed the lam to strengthen the active participle, so He said: ﴿for the zakah﴾, i.e., for the purification, which is the giving of zakah, or for the discharge of zakah, which is the greatest confirmer of faith, ﴿are doers﴾, so that they might gather in the purity of religion between the heart, the body and wealth.

Ibn Kathir said: This (surah) is Meccan, and zakah was only made obligatory in Medina in the second year of the Hijrah. The apparent meaning is that what was made obligatory in Medina was the zakah with fixed prescribed amounts (dhat al-nisab), and that the origin of zakah was already obligatory in Mecca, as Allah the Exalted said in Surat al-An'am:

﴿And give its due on the day of its harvest﴾ [al-An'am: 141].

(p-108)

When he had indicated that spending wealth in its proper place is purification, and withholding it from that is ruin, he followed it with an allusion that spending the private part in other than its proper place is impurity, and guarding it is purity. So he said: ﴿And those who guard their private parts﴾ in intercourse and what is close to it, outwardly and inwardly, ﴿are guarding,﴾ meaning constantly, not following its desire, but rather they stand over it, humbling it and restraining it. Mentioning it after vain talk, which calls to it, and after spending wealth, which is among its greatest causes, is of great relevance.

Then He made an exception to that, saying: ﴿Except from their spouses﴾, those who have come to own their private parts through a contract of marriage. Because of the elevated status of the (marital) bond, He expressed it with "upon" (ʿalā). ﴿Or what their right hands possess﴾, meaning the ownership (riqābah) over the concubines (sarāri), and He expressed it with "what" (mā) because of their closeness to that which does not reason, given their deficiency compared to free women, who are themselves deficient compared to men. ﴿Then they are not blameworthy﴾, meaning: regarding the giving of their private parts in that case, provided it is in its proper manner.

Since whoever does not content himself with what is lawful burdens himself and seeks what harms him, he (al-Biqa'i) follows this with a statement expressing the remedy by what conveys it: ﴿So whoever seeks beyond that﴾, i.e., seeks transgressively, ﴿beyond that﴾ — the great benefit (of lawful marriage and what is owned) whose exception was stated — by fornication, sodomy, self-gratification (istimna' by hand), bestiality, or other things, ﴿those are the transgressors﴾, i.e., those who go to excess in transgressing the limits (hudud), because of what such conduct produces: the confusion of lineages, the violation of honour, the squandering of wealth, and the kindling of evil among people.

(p-109) When this was among the great trusts, he followed it with their general sense, saying: ﴿And those who are, to their trusts,﴾ that is, in matters of the private parts and others, whether they are between them and Allah, such as the prayer and the fast and others, or in the inner meanings such as sincerity (ikhlas) and truthfulness (sidq), or between them and the creatures, such as deposits (wada'i') and goods (bada'i'). So it is incumbent upon the servant to fulfill all of them, as al-Razi said. And since the covenant ('ahd) is the greatest trust, he followed it with it, drawing attention to its greatness, saying: ﴿and to their covenant, are upholders﴾ that is, those who guard it with maintenance, care and upkeep.

Now that prayer was the most exalted and most emphasized of the matters of religion that had been mentioned, and it is among the hidden matters over which trust was placed, given that God has lightened it for this community by making its time and place broad, He said: ﴿And those who are attentive to their prayers﴾, the prayers by which they were described as being humble, ﴿guard﴾, meaning they renew their observance of them with the utmost diligence, leaving out nothing of their obligatory or recommended parts, and striving for their perfections. It is read in the reading of Hamzah and al-Kisa'i in the singular (ṣalāh) to denote the category, while in the reading of the rest of the Companions' transmitted readings (al-Jama'ah) it is in the plural to indicate their numbers and types. It is not hidden what there is in beginning and closing these descriptions with prayer of glorifying it, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Know that the best of your deeds is the prayer."

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 23, verse 10:

When he had mentioned the totality of these great attributes, he magnified their reward, saying: ﴿Those are the inheritors﴾, meaning: those who have attained the highest level of excellence (al-ihsan), ﴿they﴾ exclusively (p-110) ﴿who will inherit﴾, meaning: those deserving of this description, which indicates their survival after their enemies, so that they inherit the abode of Allah due to their nearness to Him and their being singled out for it, after their inheritance of the land of this world, over which they contended, despite their being killed and weakened, against our enemies, the disbelievers, despite their numbers and strength. So the final outcome was theirs in it, as We wrote in the Psalms: ﴿That the earth shall be inherited by My righteous servants﴾ [al-Anbiya': 105]. ﴿We will surely destroy the wrongdoers﴾ [Ibrahim: 13]. ﴿And We will surely make you dwell in the land after them﴾ [Ibrahim: 14].

﴿Those who inherit the Firdaws﴾, which is the highest part of Paradise. Originally, it means a great, wide garden that gathers the finest plants and trees, including grapevines and whatever resembles them, from all that is found in gardens and in valleys containing various kinds of vegetation. They take possession of it after the Resurrection, along with the dwellings Allah has prepared for them therein, and what He had prepared for the disbelievers had they believed, or had they not gone out (of Paradise) when their two parents went out of it. ﴿They﴾ specifically, ﴿therein﴾, meaning not in any other place, ﴿abide forever﴾. These verses are the most comprehensive of what is mentioned in describing the believers.

Imam Ahmad narrated in his Musnad (a collection of hadith arranged by the companion narrators), and al-Tirmidhi in the Tafsir section of his Jami' (a comprehensive hadith collection), from ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: "When revelation descended upon the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), a sound like the humming of bees could be heard near his face. One day it came down to him, and we remained a while. Then he faced the qiblah, raised his hands, and said: 'O Allah, increase us and do not diminish us, honor us and do not humiliate us, give to us and do not deprive us, prefer us and do not prefer others over us, be pleased with us and make us pleased.' Then he said: 'Ten verses have been revealed to me; whoever observes them will enter Paradise.' Then he recited ﴿Successful indeed are the believers﴾ [al-Muminun: 1] until he finished the ten."

Al-Nasa'i narrated it in the Book of Prayer (al-Salah) and said: "Munkar (a rejected report); no one is known to have narrated it except Yunus ibn Sulaym, and Yunus is not known." Abu Hayyan attributed the end of the hadith to al-Hakim in al-Mustadrak.

Imam Abu Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr said: He (Allah) elaborated at the opening of this surah what He had summarized in His saying ﴿O you who believe, bow and prostrate and worship your Lord and do good﴾ [al-Hajj: 77]. He informed about what the one who bows and prostrates should be committed to in terms of humility (khushu'). For the connection between the two passages: the first came as a command and the second as praise and a description of what completes the state. It is as if, when He commanded the believers and made success a hope as a reward for their compliance, it was likely that they would ask about the details of the worship and good deeds He had commanded, through which their success is completed. So it was said to him: "The successful one is the one who is committed to such-and-such." He mentioned seven kinds of worship, which are foundations for what lies beyond them and which entail all the other obligations. He has explained the ruling on each of these acts of worship and what relates to them in the Book and the Sunnah. Since maintaining the prayer is incompatible with committing any sin at all (﴿Indeed, prayer forbids immorality and wrongdoing﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 45]), for this reason these acts of worship were not closed with it, after alerting to the place of prayer among these acts of worship by mentioning humility in it first. These seven kinds were followed by mention of seven stages through which a person passes before coming out into this world. So He said: ﴿And We certainly created man from an extract of clay﴾ [al-Muminun: 12], up to His saying: ﴿Then We produced him as another creation. So blessed is Allah, the best of creators﴾ [al-Muminun: 14]. It is as if it had been said to him: "Your creation and your coming out into the world were only completed after these seven transformations, and you are only freed from your worldly life by committing to these seven acts of worship." Immediately following these verses is His saying ﴿And We have created above you seven paths﴾ [al-Muminun: 17]. Perhaps this confirms this consideration, and it is brought for its relevance, and Allah knows best. Just as the beginning of this surah explains what was summarized in the verses before it, so too the verses after it elaborate the summary of what preceded in His saying ﴿O mankind, if you are in doubt about the Resurrection, then indeed We created you from dust, then from a drop [of semen]﴾ [al-Hajj: 5]. This suffices for the connection between the two surahs, and Allah, glorified is He, is the One sought for help.

When He, glory be to Him, mentioned Paradise, which implies the mention of resurrection (al-Ba'th), He argued for the power to resurrect by pointing to the creation of man at the beginning, and then to what is greater than him, the cosmos (al-Akwan) and the benefits in both. When this was established, He began to warn those who were arrogant towards it by destroying those who came before, and He began with the story of Nuh, peace be upon him, because he was the first, and because his salvation was in the Ark (al-Fulk), which is the one sealed by the verse before it. In this there is a reminder of the blessing of salvation (p-113) in it, since all of them are of his offspring. When the complete power to choose was established through the threat of destroying those who came before, He warned the Arabs of a punishment like that. When the deterrent of warning with punishments was complete, He turned to appealing for gratitude for blessings, by distinguishing man above the rest of the animals and similar things. Then He returned to the proofs of the power to resurrect through His oneness and His transcendence above partners and offspring, to the end of them. Then, in the beginning of the surah that follows, He mentioned, as He has mentioned here, the guarding of private parts, so He mentioned the ruling on whoever does not guard his private part and followed it with what is suitable of its consequences.

Since the implied meaning is: "We have certainly decreed the resurrection of all the servants after death, a group of them to bliss and a group to the Hellfire, and We are able to restore them, even if you are torn apart and become dust, for dust has a root in life, just as We were able to originate them. Indeed We created your father Adam from the dust of the earth before dust had any root in life," He linked to it His saying, indicating this implied meaning and offering it as evidence for resurrection, manifesting Himself in the station of greatness, emphasising it to establish for them, because of their denial of resurrection, the station of those who deny: ﴿And We certainly created man﴾, that is, this species which you witness, content in himself, happy with his action and his sense, ﴿from an extract﴾ (p-114), that is, a small thing, as the form of the word indicates, like the parings and the sweepings, which We drew out and extracted gently, so that it was at the utmost of moderation, and it is the clay of Adam, peace be upon him, which He drew out with His gentleness, ﴿from clay﴾, that is, of the same kind as the clay of the earth. Imam Ahmad, Abu Dawud and al-Tirmidhi narrated from Abu Musa, may Allah be pleased with him, from the Prophet (ﷺ) who said: "Allah created Adam from a handful which He took from all the earth, so the children of Adam came according to the extent of the earth: among them came the red, the white and the black, and what is between that; and the wicked and the good, and what is between that."

When He, glory be to Him, mentioned the first origin of the human being, which is the clay that He honoured by combining the two purifiers in it, and He expressed it with *creation* (*khalq*) because of the mixing it contains, since *khalq*, as already explained by al-Harali (al-Ḥarālī) at the beginning of Surat al-Baqara, is the determining of the mixed components of what is intended to appear as a form after blending and composition, yet it is not something that follows the wisdom of causation that we know, namely that a human being should come from clay. He then followed it with its second origin, which is the purest of the two purifiers (*ṭuhūrayn*): water, from which every living thing is made. He expressed it with *ja'l* (making/placing), because, as also explained earlier, it denotes the manifestation of a cause and its transformation. What comes from clay (p-115) that results from water and is drawn from it is simple, with no mixture in it, so it has no creation (*takhlīq*) of its own. He expressed the sequence with the particle of delay (*tarākhī*), because turning clay into water is very improbable. So He said: ﴿Then We made it﴾, meaning the clay, or this type extracted from what was created from clay, by developing its individuals with wondrous craftsmanship and subtle arrangement, ﴿a drop of semen﴾, meaning fluid water pouring forth with no trace of clay in it, ﴿in a firm place﴾, meaning between the backbone and the ribs, then the womb, the word being a verbal noun used as the name of the place, ﴿secure﴾, meaning protected from harmful things.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 23, verse 14:

Since the transformation of water into blood is an extraordinary matter that lies beyond ordinary causation, and since the drop (nutfah), which is the origin of the human being, sometimes decays and at other times begins to develop, He expressed it with "creation" (khalq) because of what He mixes with it, of what it acquires from the womb at the time of its reddening, and He joined it with the particle of delay (thumma), saying: ﴿Then﴾, that is, after an interval in time and an elevation in rank and greatness, ﴿We created﴾, that is, by the greatness that belongs to Us, ﴿the drop﴾, that is, the very white one, ﴿a clinging clot﴾, red, blood that is thick, intensely red, congealed and solid.

Since what follows the clot consists of ascending stages, each one causing the next by the decree of the Mighty, the All-Knowing, a decree that is specific to Him without any delay, and since its causation is not a habit that anyone other than Him, glorified is He, is able to perform, He expressed it with the particle of sequence (fa') and with "creation," saying: ﴿So We created the clot into a lump of flesh﴾, that is, a small piece of flesh with no form in it and no outline. ﴿Then We created the lump of flesh﴾ by refining it and hardening it with the heat and the subtle, obscure matters that We caused to be in it, ﴿into bones﴾, from a head, two legs, and what lies between them. ﴿Then We clothed﴾ with the power of origination that belongs to Us, ﴿the bones with flesh﴾, by what We produced from them, returning them to their state before they became bone, so We covered those bones, strengthened them, and firmed them up with the ligaments and sinews.

Since the shaping and the breathing in of the spirit are of such great majesty, of whatever kind, He indicated it by His saying: ﴿Then We brought him into being﴾, that is, this one spoken of, by Our greatness, ﴿as another creation﴾, that is, a great, glorious creature, moving, speaking, a clear adversary, very far removed from clay. Al-Razi said: The root nun-shin-hamza indicates the elevation and loftiness of something.

Since this detailed account of the development of the human being is a cause for magnifying the Creator: ﴿So blessed is﴾, that is, He is established with an establishment that nothing can establish, in that He possesses all the attributes of perfection and is exalted above every trace of deficiency, so He is capable of everything; and if any shade of incapacity had approached Him, He would not be perfectly established. For this reason He said: ﴿Allah﴾, expressing by the proper name that comprises all the Most Beautiful Names; and He indicated the beauty of the human being by His saying: ﴿the best of creators﴾, that is, of those who measure, meaning that He measured this wondrous creation with this measure, then developed it through its stages, between an infant nursing, a strong adolescent, a vigorous youth, a mighty man, and a decrepit elder, and to what lies between these of affairs that none encompasses except the Subtle, the All-Aware.

Since the causing of death of what has become this way, after great strength and complete perception, is among the marvels, and since its existence in him and its recurrence upon him at every time has made it a familiar matter and an apparent, uncovered thing, and since man's insolence toward his Creator, his rebellion, and his opposition to His command amount to forgetting this familiar matter, as if denying it, He pointed to that by His saying, exalted is He, causative and emphatic in confirmation: ﴿Then indeed you﴾. And since it is possible that the contingent has nothing from its own essence except nonexistence, He removed the preposition and said: ﴿after that﴾, i.e., after that great matter of being described by life and of being given extension of life in varying terms, ﴿will surely die﴾. By this description he pointed to the fact that death is a established matter for the human being, living during his life, inseparable from him; indeed, there is nothing for a contingent in its own essence except nonexistence.

Once the power to resurrect has been established in a way that no sane person could doubt, He said, negating what the adverbial placement of the prepositional phrase might suggest: ﴿Then indeed you﴾. He specified the greatest, complete resurrection, which is the locus of reward and punishment, because whoever acknowledges what is less than it, such as life in the grave and other things, [still needs to be told]. So He said: ﴿on the Day of Resurrection﴾, that is, the Day on which all creatures are gathered, ﴿you will be raised﴾. He omitted the emphasis on death to draw attention to its being evident, but He did not leave the statement without emphasis, because it runs contrary to habit. Nor does mention of this imply a denial of life in the grave at the time of questioning.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 23, verse 17:

When He had shown them that their own reflection upon themselves suffices them, and that belief in resurrection concerns them, He followed it with another proof, by reminding them of the creation of what is greater than them, and of His management of them through His creation and the creation of the benefits within it for their sustenance. So He said: ﴿And We have created above you﴾ in the whole direction of above, at a height you do not truly grasp ﴿seven﴾ and, to express magnificence, He used a plural of multitude, saying ﴿paths (ṭarā'iq)﴾, that is, heavens that do not change from the state in which We have ordered them until We will. Some of them are above others, fitting closely together, and each one is on a path peculiar to it, and in them are paths for their stars. The Imam ʿAbd al-Ḥaqq al-Ishbīlī said in his book al-Wā'ī: "They were called ṭarā'iq because they strike against one another (muṭāraqa), one following upon the trace of another." End of quotation.

This is from their saying: "So-and-so is on one ṭarīqa," meaning one state, and "this is the miṭrāq of that," meaning its follower and its counterpart, and "a ṭirāq feather," when some of it is above other parts. Ibn al-Qaṭṭāʿ said: "The wing of the bird was uṭriqa," meaning in the passive form: the upper feathers were clothed over the lower ones. Abū ʿUbayd al-Harawī said: "The wing of the bird was uṭriqa" when one feather falls upon the one beneath it and clothes it, and "in its feathers are ṭuruq" when some of them ride upon others. Al-Ṣaghānī said in Majmaʿ al-Baḥrayn: "Ṭaraq, with a fatḥa on the ṭāʾ, also means in feathers that some of them are above others." Ibn al-Athīr said in al-Nihāya: "ṭāraqa the sandal" means when he made it layer upon layer, joining some of it upon others. In al-Qāmūs: "al-ṭirāq, like kitāb, is every patch with which a sandal is stitched, so that it is equal to its pattern, and a hide is hollowed to the size of a shield and stuck onto the shield." Al-Qazzāz said: "It is said: a shield is muṭraq when this is made for it." Al-Ṣaghānī said in al-Majmaʿ: "And al-majānn al-miṭraqa is the one whose parts strike upon one another, like the muṭraqa sandal, that is, stitched part upon part." It is said: "it was uṭriqat with hide and sinew," meaning it was clothed. Abū ʿUbayd said: "ṭāraqa the sandal" when he made patches upon patches. He said concerning khaṣf: it is the folding of a layer over a layer, and the root of khaṣf is joining and gathering. Al-Qazzāz said: "And I ṭāraqtu between the two sandals or the two garments," meaning I put one of them over the other. End of quotation. The root of ṭarq is striking.

Although the heavens strike one another, one above another, they are also ṭuruq (paths) for the angels, who descend through them by His command, glory be to Him and exalted.

Since neglecting a thing after bringing it into existence would be heedlessness toward it, and since resurrection is the introduction of a management that did not exist before, as death is likewise, He clarified that such noble acts are His customary practice, to manifest power and to declare Himself free from incapacity and heedlessness. So He said: ﴿And We were not﴾, that is, by what We possess of greatness, ﴿heedless of the creation﴾, that is, what We created and finished bringing into existence, and of bringing into being what did not exist, by Our complete power and encompassing knowledge ﴿heedless﴾. Rather, We have managed it with a firm management, tied it to causes from which effects arise by which its welfare is achieved. We placed in every heaven what ought to be in it of benefits, and likewise in every earth, and We preserved it from corruption until the time in which We will fold this world and bring forth another. Yet along with that, We are every day in a matter, and manifesting a proof. We know what enters the earth and what comes out of it, and what descends from the sky and what ascends into it. If We will, We let the cause take effect, and the effect arises from it; and if We will, We withhold it from what has been prepared for it. So none of that occurs except by a new creation. How then could it be supposed of Us that We would leave creation after their death in vain, when among them is the obedient whose reward We have not yet paid, and the disobedient upon whom We have not yet sent punishment? Or how could We not be able to restore them to what they were after We had already been able to originate them when they were nothing?

And We sent down water from the sky in measure (p-121), i.e., by Our majesty, ﴿from the sky﴾, i.e., from its direction, ﴿water in measure﴾, perhaps—and God knows best—in the measure that waters the crops and trees, revives the wastelands and deserts, and supplies what the seas need of what the rivers pour into them; for if it were more than that, the seas would flood the regions, and if it were less than that, it would lead to the drying up of plants and trees. ﴿Then We made it settle﴾ by Our majesty ﴿in the earth﴾, part of it on its surface and part in its depths; We did not make all of the earth share in what is on its surface, nor did We make what is in its depths hidden, so that its benefit might be general and access to it might be easy. ﴿And indeed We﴾, with the greatness that belongs to Us, ﴿are able to take it away﴾, i.e., able to remove it in every kind of removal, by every means—by corruption, by lifting it up, by sinking it deep, and otherwise—together with removing the blessing that is found with those with whom We are. ﴿Indeed We are capable﴾ with a power that is at the utmost of greatness. So beware of exposing yourselves to what angers Us.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 23, verse 19:

When He mentioned His sending down (of water), He made it a consequence (sabbaba 'anhu) an evidence (al-dalil) of nearness to the Resurrection (al-ba'th), so He said: ﴿Then We brought forth⁠﻿ — that is, We caused to come out and gave life — ﴾ ﴿for you⁠﻿ — specifically, not for Us — ﴾ ﴿by means of it⁠﻿ — that is, by that water from which We made every living thing ﴾ ﴿gardens⁠﻿ — that is, orchards that conceal (tajunn, i.e., screen) what is within them ﴾ ﴿of date palms and grapevines⁠﻿. He specified these two kinds because of their nobility, and because they are the most abundant of fruits among the Arabs. The first was named after its tree (bi-ism shajaratihi) because of the many beneficial purposes in it, unlike the second, since the second is the intended purpose of its tree. He indicated other fruits with His saying: ﴿For you⁠﻿ — that is, specifically — ﴾ ﴿therein⁠﻿, that is, in the gardens, ﴾ ﴿are many fruits⁠﻿, and for you therein are other than these.

Since the implied sense was: "from them, while fresh, you enjoy (tatafakkahun)," He followed it with His saying: ﴿and from them⁠﻿ — that is, after drying and pressing — ﴾ ﴿you eat⁠﻿, that is, eating is renewed for you through preservation. Perhaps He placed the adverbial phrase first to magnify the favor (imtinan) of it.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 23, verse 20:

When He, glory be to Him, mentioned that which, when pressed, becomes water that is not useful for condiment (*iṣṭibāḥ*), He followed it with that which, when pressed, becomes oil that serves both condiment and dipping (*iṣṭibāgh*). He separated it from the former because it is more indicative of power, so He said: ﴿And a tree﴾, meaning, *and We brought forth by it a tree*, namely the olive tree, ﴿that grows out of Mount﴾

Since the context concerns the provision of blessings, the word *madd* (extension, abundance) suited it, so He said: ﴿Sinai﴾. The Hafiz 'Imad al-Din Ibn Kathir said: It is *Tur Sinin*, the mountain on which God spoke to Moses son of 'Imran, peace be upon him, and the mountains around it, in which there are olive trees. The author of the *al-Qamus* said: *al-Tur* means a mountain. There is a mountain near Ayla, which is attributed to Sinai and Sinin; a mountain in al-Sham; and it is said that it is the one attributed to Sinai. There is a mountain in al-Quds (Jerusalem) to the right of the mosque, and another to its south, where the tomb of Harun (Aaron), peace be upon him, is located, overlooking Ras al-'Ayn; and another overlooking Tiberias. End of quotation. It is a compound noun made of two words. It is also said that it is rather *mudaf* (in construct) to Sina'. The meaning of Sina' is "beauty"; it is said "blessed"; it is said it is a well-known stone; it is said it is a tree. Perhaps He singled it out from among the mountains because it is near those addressed first by this Qur'an, namely the Arabs; and because of the strangeness of olive trees growing there, since it is a land of heat, whereas the olive is a plant of cold lands; and because it is pure in that its vegetation is of what descends from the sky as water, owing to its extreme height. It is also far-fetched to claim that the moisture in it comes from the sea. For the Imam Abu al-'Abbas Ahmad Ibn al-Qass, one of the early companions of al-Shafi'i, reported in his book *Adillat al-Qibla* that one ascends to its summit by six thousand, six hundred and sixty-six steps. He said: They are like steps cut into rock. When one reaches halfway up the path, one arrives at a level area on the ground in which there are trees and sweet water. At this place there is a church named after the Prophet Elijah, peace be upon him, and in it is a cave. It is said that when Elijah, peace be upon him, fled from the king Izqil, he hid in it. Then one ascends from this place by the steps until one reaches the top of the mountain, and at its peak there is a church built in the name of Moses, peace be upon him, with marble pillars; its doors are of brass and iron, and its roof is of pine wood, and above its roofs are sheets of lead, tightly sealed with the utmost care. In it there is only one monk, who prays, burns incense and lights its lamps, and no one can sleep there at all. This monk has made for himself a small house outside the church in which he lives. This church was built on the spot where God spoke to Moses, peace be upon him. Around it, that is, around the mountain, at its base, there are six thousand monasteries and hermitages for monks and worshippers. The tribute of Egypt used to be carried to them in the days of the Roman kingdom to meet the expenses of the monasteries and others. Today there are only about seventy monks there, who dwell in the monastery inside the fortress; and most of the rest is inhabited by the Bedouins of the Banu Ramada. On the mountain there are a hundred hermitages. The trees of this mountain are almond and cypress. When you descend from the Tur, you come upon a steep path from which you descend a few steps and arrive at the monastery of the Christian *Hussayn*, which has a wall of carved stone with battlements and two iron gates. In the middle of this monastery is a spring of sweet water, and around this spring there is a brass railing so that no one falls into it. Lead pipes have been arranged through which the water flows to the vineyards they have around the monastery. It is said that this monastery is the place where Moses, peace be upon him, saw the fire in the bush (*al-'Ulayq*), and the qibla of those who are there is the back of the Ka'ba. In it, (p-125) someone says:

*"The Tur marvelled at your steadfastness, O Moses, when He addressed you with the sublime speech."*

The Tur is among the districts of Egypt; from it to the town of Qulzum by land is a four-day journey, and from it to Fustat in Egypt is a seven-day journey. End of the words of Ibn al-Qass.

I myself asked someone who has knowledge of the mentioned mountain: Are there olive trees on it? He informed me that he had not seen any of them on it, but had seen them in the lowlands around it, and they are numerous, and their olives, despite their size, are better than others. If that is so, it is stranger than if they were on it, for because of its height it is colder than what is lower on the earth, so it is more fitting for them. It appeared to me, and God knows best, that the wisdom of God, exalted be He, in determining that the number of steps should be what was mentioned, is to correspond the time of the first creation to the place of the first preservation. That is because God, exalted be He, created the heavens and the earth in six days, which is the first creation; He spoke to Moses, peace be upon him, and wrote the Tablets for him on this mountain; then He completed for him the Torah, which is the greatest of the books after the Qur'an. The system of the first preservation is the heavenly books and the divine laws, as has preceded in al-Fatiha, al-An'am and al-Kahf.

When He, glory be to Him, reminded of the bringing forth of this tree on this mountain, far from the waters of the seas because of its height and firmness, or because of the hot land around it, He mentioned its distinction from (p-126) the common trees in another, wondrous way, so He said: ﴿grows﴾, that is, by the water which has no oil in it at all, as growth (*nabāt*) according to the recitation of the majority; or as causing growth (*inbāt*) according to the recitation (*qira'a*) of Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and Warsh from Ya'qub, with a *ḍamma* on the first letter, ﴿with the oil﴾ its fruit being coated with it. It is in origin a light, viscous, fluid substance that separates and does not mix with the water that is its source, so it is used for lamps and anointing. It seems He specified it because it is the most excellent and most perfect of oils.

Since what is eaten from it is the oil, and the olive before pressing, He conjoined with a particle indicating continuity, so He said: ﴿and a condiment﴾, that is, it grows with something that colours (*yuṣbigh*), meaning *yulawwin*, the bread when one dips in it or eats with it, ﴿for the eaters﴾. He used the indefinite form for it, perhaps because there are other condiments more noble and more delicious than it, although its blessing is well known. The Imam Ahmad narrated from Abu Usayd Malik ibn Rabi'a al-Sa'idi al-Ansari, may God be pleased with him, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Eat olive oil and anoint yourselves with it, for it comes from a blessed tree."

And al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Majah and 'Abd ibn Humayd in his *Musnad* and *Tafsir*, as quoted by Ibn Kathir, related from Ibn 'Umar, may God be pleased with them both, that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Eat with olive oil and anoint yourselves with it, for it comes out of a blessed tree." Abu Hayyan said: He singled out these three kinds, the date palm, the grape and the olive, because they are the noblest of trees and the most comprehensive in benefits.

When God, glorified and exalted is He, had shown His power through what He brings to life by water, a life limited in comparison with the soul, He followed it with what He bestows upon them in the way of complete life, saying: ﴿And indeed, in the livestock there is surely a lesson for you﴾, namely the camels, cattle and sheep. ﴿A lesson﴾ by which you pass from the outward aspect of their condition to its inner reality, concerning the perfect power of God, exalted is He, over resurrection and other things. Then He began a detailed account of the lesson they contain, saying: ﴿We give you to drink﴾. Since "livestock" (al-an'am) is singular in form because it is a collective noun (ism jam'), and what is drunk from it is not mentioned, the pronoun is made feminine according to the meaning, and it is understood that what is intended is what yields milk specifically, which is the females. This is an device called istikhdam (using one word in two senses), because if all that the name applies to were intended, the pronoun would be masculine. Therefore He said: ﴿from what is in their bellies﴾, meaning: We make it for you a drink beneficial to the body, agreeable to the appetite, which you enjoy, and which comes out from between the digesta and the blood, as has passed in Surat al-Nahl. ﴿And in them for you﴾, meaning in the herds of livestock, and the prepositional phrase is placed first to magnify their benefits, to the extent that anything other than them seems as nothing (p-128) ﴿are many benefits﴾, through their submission to what is wanted from them, which is not easily obtained from smaller animals, and through their offspring, their wool and their hair, and other traces of them.

Since the sense was: you employ them for those benefits, He joined to it, placing the prepositional phrase first to magnify what is eaten from them, saying: ﴿And from them you eat﴾, easily and without any refusal regarding any of that. Had He willed, He would have prevented them from this and given you power over them. Had He willed, He would have made their flesh not ripen, or made it a filth not to be eaten. But by His power and knowledge He prepared them for what has been mentioned and made them tractable for you.

Since the differences among animals in their strengths and in how readily they submit to being led are evidence of the perfection of power, and since carrying oneself and one's goods upon them, and upon other animals, is among the greatest benefits, without which most interests would be brought to nothing, He reminded them of it here, alluding to other land-carriers, and explicitly mentioning the carriers of the sea. So He said, placing first the prepositional phrase ʿalayhā (upon them), which, relative to the carrying of other things by comparison with the carrying of these, is for its great impact as good as nonexistent: ﴿And upon them﴾, that is, upon the cattle suitable for carrying, of camels and cattle, on land, ﴿and upon the ship﴾ at sea. And since it is known from their being made subservient, despite their greatness and strength, while others are unable to do so despite their smallness and weakness, that there is no doer of that except Allah (p-129), even though the favour being bestowed is the carrying itself and not in regard to anything else, He made the verb passive in His saying ﴿you are carried﴾, by His bestowing this upon you. And had He willed, He would have prevented it. So remember the greatness of His power and the perfection of His craftsmanship, magnify Him with the magnification that is His due, give Him thanks for what He has granted you of those blessings, and devote the religion sincerely to Him, that you may prosper and so be among the inheritors.

The estimated sense is: "So We certainly carried Noah, and whomever We willed from among those who believed in him, including his offspring, his family and others, upon the ark, and We drowned all who opposed him among the people of the earth, entirely, by Our power. We granted him victory over them after his weakness before them, by Our hands and Our might, and We made him and his descendants the inheritors. You were the offspring in their loins, and We multiplied them until they filled the earth with them, as evidence of what We had previously set forth of Our singularity. Thus We have made it customary for this Noble Book to mention the mighty seizing after the proofs of Divine Oneness. We then followed him with the messengers of whom you have heard and whose reports you have come to know. O you who now deny the messengership of humans because you deny the messengership of this Noble Prophet! It is linked to what precedes, threatening with the destruction of earlier peoples so that they will turn back from disbelief, reminding of the blessing of deliverance so that they will turn to gratitude, and consoling this Noble Prophet and those believers with him regarding those prophets who were denied before him and whose followers were harmed. It also shows that He prefers whom He wills among His servants with messengership, just as He preferred the clay of humankind over the rest of the clays, and that success through inheritance and a good life in both abodes is specific to the believers, as He mentioned at the beginning of the surah. He mentioned Noah (p-١٣٠) because his story is the most famous of stories, because his people filled the earth and their multitude did not avail them and their strength did not benefit them, and because he is the second father after the first father, who was indicated by the clay, and because his deliverance and the deliverance of the believers with him was by means of the ark, which was sealed with the sign before him. So He said: ﴿And We certainly sent﴾, a form in the plural of majesty indicating increased consolation, that He had given him signs such that humankind believed in the like of them, and this Prophet ﷺ fulfilled that fully. ﴿Noah﴾, that is, he is the second father after Adam, peace be upon them both, ﴿to his people﴾, and they were all the inhabitants of the earth, because of the connection among them through their being of one language. ﴿He said﴾, that is, as a consequence he said: ﴿O my people﴾, showing gentleness toward them, ﴿worship Allah﴾, that is, the Supreme King, to whom none is equal, alone, because He alone is your God, due to His deserving all qualities of perfection. He began, by way of explanation, with His words: ﴿You have no﴾ and he went to the extreme in negation with what is the right of worship, saying: ﴿deity﴾, that is, a worshipped one in truth, ﴿other than Him﴾, so do not worship anything besides Him.

Since the proofs of Divine Oneness and greatness, through the granting of reward and the imposition of punishment, are wholly evident and need no deep reflection, it follows that he denounced their feeling secure from His scheme and their not fearing His harm, saying: ﴿Will you not then be wary?﴾, that is, will you not fear what ought to be feared, so that you take for yourselves a protection from His punishment, and act (p-١٣١) by what piety requires, namely devoting worship to Him alone, out of fear of His harm to you and hope for His benefit to you.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 23, verse 24:

﴿Then said﴾, that is, as a consequence of that, they denied him. So ﴿the chiefs﴾, that is, the nobles whose sight fills the hearts with awe, ﴿who disbelieved﴾ from among his people. Since all the people of faith at that time were one tribe, being united in one language, He placed first the words ﴿who disbelieved﴾, that is, in God, because consolation through explaining the denial is more complete. The relative clause here is short, and no ambiguity or weakness in the composition arises from it, unlike what comes later. It seems their clans were distinct, so He increased the reproach against them by making known that they were among the people closest to him, through their saying: ﴿This is only a human being like yourselves﴾, that is, Noah, peace be upon him, ﴿who wants to excel over you﴾, that is, wants to assume superiority by claiming such a thing, ﴿over you﴾, so that you would become his followers, and there is no special privilege for him in this over you.

Since the implication was: "So God did not send him, as he claimed," He joined to it their saying: ﴿If God had willed﴾, that is, the Supreme King, to send to you and not to worship other than Him, ﴿He would have sent down﴾ for that purpose ﴿angels﴾. And they did not know that the One Able to give some substances precedence by making them angels is able to give precedence to whomever He wills, and with whatever He wills, among the angels and others.

Since this implies the denial of human prophethood, they stated it explicitly in their saying, falsely and slanderously, just as Pharaoh and his household denied when they said the like of this statement, and as they denied the believer concerning the prophethood of Joseph, peace be upon him: ﴿We have not heard of this﴾, that is, of sending a prophet from among humans who forbids worshipping other than God for the purpose of drawing near to Him. Thus they made God a stone, and deemed it impossible for a prophet to be human, ﴿among our forefathers of old﴾, and we have not heard of what he calls to of monotheism.

When they denied him the prophethood and confined his aim to seeking leadership (siyadah), and their being subordinate to him in this manner was, in their view, something impossible, they said: "﴿He is only a man who has madness in him﴾", meaning: he is merely a man with jinnah (madness, jununn) in his intention, in that he seeks to show superiority by means that will breed hatred for him and humiliation for them, and we know no specific purpose for it that would be particular to him; so we will never obey him in this. "﴿So wait for him﴾", meaning: as a consequence of the ruling that he is mad, we command you to refrain from him, since there is no blame upon a madman. "﴿Until a time﴾", meaning: until a period in which he may recover his senses or die.

So it was as if it were said: "Then what did he say?" It was answered: ﴿He said﴾ when he despaired of their believing: ﴿"My Lord, help me"﴾, that is, support me against them, ﴿"because they deny me"﴾, that is, because of their denying me, for denying the messenger is a belittling of the one who sent him.

(p-133) ﴿So We revealed to him﴾, meaning that as a consequence of his supplication, We revealed to him, ﴿"Build the ship"﴾.

Since he feared their harm to him in his work of building it, and otherwise, He said: ﴿"under Our eyes"﴾, meaning that nothing of your affairs or theirs is hidden from Us, and you know Our power over them. So trust in Our protection and do not fear anything from them. Since he did not know that craft, He said: ﴿"and by Our inspiration"﴾. Then He confirmed for him their destruction and its nearness by His saying: ﴿"So when Our command comes"﴾, meaning the destruction, immediately after you finish from it, ﴿"and the oven gushes forth"﴾. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: it is the surface of the earth. In the al-Qamus (a lexicon): al-tannur is the oven in which bread is baked, and the surface of the earth, and every spring of water, and a mountain near al-Muṣaiṣa, end of quote.

The more fitting interpretation of this matter is to take it as the oven in which one bakes, so that it is a sign within a sign. ﴿Then embark﴾, meaning enter, ﴿therein﴾, meaning the ship, ﴿two of each pair﴾ of the animals, ﴿two﴾, male and female, ﴿and your family﴾, of your children and others, ﴿except those against whom the word has already gone forth﴾, not for him, ﴿among them﴾, of destruction, to sever the bond of kinship between you and him through disbelief.

Since the intended sense is: "Do not carry him with you and do not show compassion toward him, because of his wrongdoing," He followed it with His saying: ﴿"And do not address Me concerning those who have wronged"﴾, meaning with a request for salvation, in general. Then He gave the reason for this with His saying: ﴿"Indeed they are to be drowned"﴾, meaning that the decree has already sealed their fate, and We honor you by not receiving a request that would not be accepted.

(p. 134) When he had mentioned that, because repelling harms (*dar' al-mafasid*, preventing what is corrupt) by forbidding what does not please Allah is more important than bringing about benefits (*jalb al-masalih*), he followed it with the command to give thanks, saying: ﴿So when you settle, you and those with you﴾, i.e., are restrained, ﴿on the ship﴾, i.e., among mankind and others, ﴿then you have finished carrying out the command to load it﴾, ﴿then say﴾, because your knowledge of Allah is not like the knowledge of others, so the praise that comes from you is more complete. And when you say it, those with you follow you, since you are their example and they are in the utmost obedience to you. For this reason, after the general term in the condition, he made the response singular: ﴿Praise﴾, i.e., the encompassing of the attributes of perfection in bringing into existence and in annihilating, ﴿belongs to Allah﴾, i.e., the One who has no equal, because He alone is the one specified with the attributes of glory, ﴿who has saved us﴾ by our being carried in it, ﴿from the people﴾, the mighty and arrogant, ﴿the wrongdoers﴾, who, because they place things in other than their proper places, are in the state of one who walks in darkness. So to You is the praise after their destruction, just as there was praise to You in their emergence and their survival. The praise in this surah, which opens with the greatest rite by which the first survival is sustained, namely the prayer characterized by humility, is like the praise in the surah of the first creation, al-An'am, in His saying, may He be exalted:

﴿So the last remnant of the people who did wrong was cut off. And praise belongs to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-An'am: 45].

When he had indicated to him by this statement the safety of the carrying (on the ark), he followed it with an indication of the promise of settling him in the land, and so he said: ﴿And say: "My Lord, cause me to disembark at a blessed place, and You are the best of those who cause to disembark."﴾ "Cause me to disembark" (anzilni) refers to in the ark and then on the land, and in every station to which You bring me down and grant me its inheritance. "A place of disembarking" (munzalan) means a place of alighting, or "a disembarking" (inzalan). "Blessed" (mubarakan) means fit for one to remain in it or to be sustained by it. Since praise is the greatest stimulus to the answering of supplication, and the implied sense is "so You are the best of carriers," he joined to it his saying: ﴿And You are the best of those who cause to disembark﴾, because You suffice your guest against every distress and give him every desire he seeks.

Since this story is among the most remarkable of stories, He urged reflection upon it by His saying: ﴿Indeed in that﴾, i.e., the great matter mentioned concerning Noah and his people, and likewise what serves as a preface to it, ﴿are signs﴾, i.e., indications and proofs confirming the truthfulness of the Prophets in that the believers are the successful ones, and that they are the inheritors of the earth after the wrongdoers, however great their might and however strong their dominion. ﴿And indeed﴾, i.e., and We, with what belongs to Us of greatness, ﴿are﴾, with what belongs to Us of the established attribute indicating perfect power, ﴿testing﴾, i.e., doing the act of one who tries His servants by sending the Messengers, so that the righteous among them may become manifest from others in the world of witnessing. Then We test the righteous among them with what increases their good deeds, diminishes their evil deeds, and raises their ranks. Then We make the end [of affairs] for them, and We bring the wrongdoers to ruin with what necessitates their destruction, lays waste their dwellings, and effaces their traces. This is Our constant custom, until We inherit the earth and whoever is upon it, and there will be the manifest trial.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 23, verse 31:

When the Exalted and Glorified One had made clear their denial and the punishment with which He chastised them, and the analogy (qiyas) necessitated that whoever comes after them would fear the like of their downfall, and so would take a path other than theirs and speak other than their speech, He made clear that the lesson did not benefit them. They committed the like of their deeds and exceeded their words and actions, by the will of the Free Chooser, the One, the Subduer.

Also, since the aim, together with warning and indicating power and choice, is to indicate the singling out of the believers for success and survival after the enemies, and the destruction of the affluent (al-mutrafun) is more indicative of this, He limited Himself to mentioning them and left them unspecified, so that their story could apply to everyone among the disbelievers who claimed for himself affluence. The intended people are more likely 'Ad, since they were given, along with that, strength of bodies and greatness of physiques; and Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said so. Thamud is also intended, because of what is in al-Shu'ara' and al-Qamar that resembles some of their words here; and because the punishment of the people is expressed by the Cry (al-sayha), and because they agreed with the people of Nuh in the reason for their rejection, that he was a human being.

He omitted reporting about those after them other than denial and destruction, since there is no need to mention anything other than that. So He said: ﴿Then We produced﴾, that is, We brought into being, gave life, and raised up, by what We have of greatness.

Since they did not exhaust the time of the distance, He used the preposition and said: ﴿after them a generation﴾, that is, a community and a people.

Since perhaps one might think that they were a group of the destroyed who were saved from the punishment of the rest of them, as happens in the wars of other kings, he expressed their rescue by their creation, and established that they were newly originated after them, so He said: ﴿others﴾.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 23, verse 32:

﴿So We sent⦆ meaning: so His bringing them into being was followed by, and caused, Our sending.

Since the aim was to convey the message in a way that encompasses them, the verb was constructed with "fi" (in), indicating that he encompassed them with the message just as the contained encompasses the container, until he left none of them without making his matter clear to them. So He said: ﴿among them a Messenger from themselves﴾. By analogy, they should have hurried to follow him, since they knew what had befallen those before them on account of denial, and since they had the utmost knowledge of him because the Prophet was one of them, with the excellent qualities We had given him and the virtues with which We had adorned him, and because his honour was their honour, and because of his calling them to what is good, the goodness of which is not hidden from any sensible person and which no fair-minded person rejects. Then he explained what he was sent with by His saying: ﴿that worship Allah﴾, meaning, Him alone, because there is no equal to Him; for this reason His name was preserved, so that there is no namesake of Him. Then he gave the reason for that by His saying: ﴿you have no god other than Him﴾, and the generality was indicated by His saying: ﴿other than Him﴾.

Since the exemplary punishments had already passed before them among the deniers, and the calamities had descended upon the wrongdoers, their lack of concern and their failure to guard themselves against the like of their fates was thereby brought to account, so He said: ﴿Will you not then be wary?⦆ meaning: will you not make for yourselves a protection against what should be feared, so that you place a shield between yourselves and the wrath of Allah?

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 23, verse 33:

Since the sense is: "So they did not believe and did not fear God, [following] the way (da'b) of the people of Noah," he joined to it His saying: ﴿And the chiefs said﴾, that is, the nobles (al-ashraf), whose sight fills the hearts (alladhina tamla'u ru'yatuhumu al-sudur). Thus what is linked by the conjunction "and" is greater in consolation than what is left without it, on the assumption of a question, since this points to what it is joined to. And since the tribes had been divided by the diversity of tongues, he placed first His saying: ﴿from among his people﴾, out of concern and specification, for the sake of making the consolation complete; and also because, had he delayed it, it would have come after the completion of the relative clause, which is long. Then he explained "the chiefs" with His saying: ﴿who disbelieved﴾, that is, they concealed what they knew of the proofs of monotheism and of the retribution against the polytheists, ﴿and denied the meeting of the Hereafter﴾, because of their denial of the Resurrection.

Since luxury (taraf) is a necessary consequence of nobility, He stated it explicitly, as an indication that it—though they supposed it to be happiness in this world—is, for the most part, a cutting-off from the happiness of the Hereafter, because it carries one to insolence (ashar), exultation (batar) and arrogance (takabbur), even toward the One who bestows favour. So He said: ﴿And We had given them luxury﴾, that is, while the state was that We—by what We possess and upon what We possess of greatness—had made them prosperous ﴿in the life of this world﴾, that is, the lowly and base life, with wealth and children and abundant pleasures. They say to their followers: ﴿This is not but a human like yourselves﴾; they pointed to him in order to belittle him in the eyes of those being addressed ﴿and not but a human like you﴾, that is, in creation and in condition. Then (p-139) they described him with what suggests equality in every attribute, saying: ﴿He eats of what you eat from it﴾, of the food of this world, ﴿and drinks of what you drink﴾, that is, from its drink. So how could he be a messenger over you!

When the implied sense was: "If you follow him, you will indeed be astray," he joined to it: ﴿And if you obey a human being like yourselves﴾ in all that you see, ﴿then indeed you will be losers﴾ — that is, if you obey him, you will be defrauded (maghbunun), because you have preferred one like yourselves over yourselves in what he claims, which is something we deny.

Then they stated their denial by saying: ﴿Does he promise you that when you die and become dust and bones, you will be brought out?﴾ That is, when your souls depart from your bodies, and your bodies were (﴿kuntum﴾, "you were") ﴿dust﴾ through the dust's taking over what lies beneath their bones, and ﴿bones﴾ stripped bare. Then He stated what was promised, after having stirred the souls toward it and sent it forth in the most complete manner, and He said, substituting it for the first ﴿annakum﴾ as an elucidation of the meaning: ﴿that you will be brought out﴾, that is, from that state into which you have come, ﴿returning to what you were upon of life, with the bodies you had.﴾

Then they went on to state explicitly what the speech had implied of their remoteness-judging of that, so they said: ﴿Far, far is what you are promised﴾. That is, it is far, very far, to the point that it has become impossible. The word that follows it was not put in the nominative by it; rather it was cut off from it, for magnification of it. So it was as if it was said: "For what reason is this remoteness?" Then it was said: ﴿for what you are promised﴾.

Since they had emphasized this distancing so strongly, it was as if they had said: "We are not raised at all." Connected to this is: ﴿It is not but our life of this world﴾, that is, the only state beyond which we cannot conceive, ﴿our life of this world﴾ (p-140), that is, the one nearest to us, which is what we are in. Then they explained it with their words: ﴿We die and we live﴾, meaning that whoever exists among us dies, and others arise after them. ﴿And we are not to be resurrected﴾ after death.

So it was as if it were said: "What is this speech he is uttering?" It was said: "It is a lie." Then they confined his matter to lying, saying: ﴿It is not but﴾ — that is, he is nothing but — and they incited [their people] against abandoning the like of what he addressed them with, by their saying: ﴿a man who has fabricated﴾ — that is, who has deliberately invented ﴿against Allah﴾ — that is, the Supreme King — ﴿a lie﴾. A man ought not to do the like of that. Or [it means]: he is one man alone, that is, one should not pay attention to him. ﴿And we are not believers in him﴾ — that is, we are not ones who affirm what he tells us of the resurrection and the message.

Then he resumed his speech: ﴿My Lord﴾, that is, O You who have been good to me by sending me to them and by other kinds of nurture, ﴿help me﴾ against them, that is, bring about victory for me, ﴿because they have denied me﴾.

Then his Lord answered him, by saying: ﴿In a little while﴾, that is, from time. He emphasized its brevity by the addition of "mā" (ma): ﴿they will surely become regretful﴾ for their failure to follow you.

ولَمّا تَسَبَّبَ عَنْ دُعائِهِ أنْ تَعْقُبَ هَلاكَهُمْ، وعَدَ اللَّهُ لَهُ بِذَلِكَ، قالَ تَعالى: ﴿فَأخَذَتْهُمُ الصَّيْحَةُ﴾ أيِ الَّتِي كَأنَّها لِقُوَّتِها لا صِحِّيَّةَ إلّا هِيَ، (p-141) ويُمْكِنُ أنْ تَكُونَ عَلى بابِها فَتَكُونُ صَيْحَةُ جِبْرَئِيلَ عَلَيْهِ الصَّلاةُ والسَّلامُ ويَكُونُ القَوْمُ ثَمُودَ، ويُمْكِنُ أنْ تَكُونَ مَجازًا عَنِ العَذابِ الهائِلِ ﴿بِالحَقِّ﴾ أيْ بِالأمْرِ الثّابِتِ مِنَ العَذابِ الَّذِي أوْجَبَ لَهُمُ الَّذِي لا تُمْكِنُ مُدافَعَتُهُ لَهم ولا لِأحَدٍ غَيْرِ اللَّهِ، ولا يَكُونُ كَذَلِكَ إلّا وهو عَدْلٌ. ﴿فَجَعَلْناهُمْ﴾ بِعَظْمَتِنا الَّتِي لا تُدانِيها عَظَمَةٌ، بِسَبَبِ الصَّيْحَةِ ﴿غُثاءً﴾ (ghuthā', debris carried by a flood) كَأنَّهم أعْجازُ نَخْلٍ خاوِيَةٌ، جاثِمَيْنِ أمْواتًا يُطْرَحُونَ كَما يُطْرَحُ الغُثاءُ، وهو ما يَحْمِلُهُ السَّيْلُ مِن نَباتٍ ونَحْوِهِ فَيَسُودُ ويَبْلى فَيَصِيرُ بِحَيْثُ لا يَنْتَفِعُ بِهِ، ونَجَّيْنا رَسُولَهم ومِن مَعَهُ مِنَ المُؤْمِنِينَ، فَخابَ الكافِرُونَ، وأفْلَحَ المُؤْمِنُونَ، وكانُوا هُمُ الوارِثِينَ لِلْأرْضِ مِن بَعْدِهِمْ.

ولَمّا كانَ هَلاكُهم عَلى هَذا الوَجْهِ سَبَبًا لِهَوانِهِمْ، عَبَّرَ عَنْهُ بِقَوْلِهِ: ﴿فَبُعْدًا﴾ أيْ هَلاكًا وطَرْدًا. ولَمّا كانَ كَأنَّهُ قِيلَ: لِمَن؟ قِيلَ: لَهُمْ! ولَكِنَّهُ أظْهَرَ الضَّمِيرَ تَعْمِيمًا وتَعْلِيقًا لِلْحُكْمِ بِالوَصْفِ تَحْذِيرًا لِكُلِّ مَن تَلَبَّسَ بِهِ فَقالَ: ﴿لِلْقَوْمِ﴾ أيِ الأقْوِياءِ الَّذِي لا عُذْرَ لَهم في التَّخَلُّفِ عَنِ اتِّباعِ الرُّسُلِ والمُدافَعَةِ عَنْهم ﴿الظّالِمِينَ﴾ الَّذِينَ وضَعُوا قُوَّتَهُمُ الَّتِي كانَ يَجِبُ عَلَيْهِمْ بَذْلُها في نَصْرِ الرُّسُلِ في خِذْلانِهِمْ.

Since it was the habit of the deniers to say, in denial: "This is a hint to us of destruction, so speak plainly and do not spare any effort in bringing it upon us and hastening it toward us, for we will not abandon what we are upon for anything." The Arabs too had claimed that the custom of death for them, and the bringing into being of those after them little by little, does not break. God, the Exalted, said, rebuking them: ﴿Then We brought into being﴾, that is, by Our greatness, which neither advancing nor delaying harms. He established the preposition for what preceded, saying: ﴿after them﴾, that is, after those whom We have already mentioned, from Noah and the generation that followed him, ﴿other generations﴾.

Then He informed that He did not hasten destruction upon any of them before the term He had set for them, by His saying: ﴿No community precedes its term﴾. Perhaps He expressed it with the present tense (al-mudari') to indicate that no such thing had occurred or would occur. He alluded to universality by His saying: ﴿from a community its term﴾, meaning the term We had decreed for its destruction, ﴿nor do they delay﴾ from it. In all of them the outcome culminated in the failure of the deniers and the success of the affirmers, and in making them the inheritors after them. He reversed this order in other verses, placing "delaying" first, because there he supposed the arrival of the term, so no consideration then remains except that of postponement.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 23, verse 44:

When He had given respite to every people until time stretched long over them, and when their intellects did not guide them to what He had set up for them of proofs, and He had lavished upon them blessings, and had brought down upon the deniers before them of vengeances, He sent among them a messenger. He indicated this by the particle of delay (tarakhi) and said: ﴿Then We sent﴾, meaning after the bringing into being of each generation of them and the lengthy respite We gave them. (p-143) From here it is known that between every two messengers there is an interval (fatra), and He attributed the messengers to Himself because He is in the station of greatness, and for added consolation. So He said: ﴿Our messengers, one after another﴾, meaning one after another in succession. Al-Razi said: it derives from "watara al-qaws" (he strung the bow), because of its continuity.

Al-Baghawi said: "watartu al-khabar" means I made one part of the report follow another, with a little pause between the two reports. Al-Isfahani said: the original is "witra", and the waw was changed to a ta' as they changed it in "al-taqwa." So every messenger came to his community saying: Worship Allah; you have no god other than Him.

When it was as if it were said: "So what happened?", it was said: ﴿Every time a messenger came to a nation﴾, and since this is in the explanation of denial, He attributed the messenger to them, as a reproach to them for being singled out for honour and then refusing it, and also for the purpose of consolation, so He said: ﴿its messenger﴾, meaning with what We commanded him of tawhid.

Since most of every nation were deniers, He attributed the action to all of them, so He said: ﴿they denied him﴾, meaning just as these people did to you when you commanded them of that. ﴿So We followed up﴾ the generations, because of their denial, ﴿some of them with others﴾ in destruction. Thus We would destroy the whole nation in a single moment: some by the Shout (al-sayha), some by the quake (al-rajfa), some by the sinking into the earth (al-khasf), and some by other than that. Our seizing them in a manner contrary to custom indicates—through Our destruction of them all, the deliverance of the messengers, their truthfulness, and the difference among them in the type of punishment—that We are the ones who do that to them by Our choice, not time (al-dahr), and that We did not do that except because of their denial.

Since they had gone, and nothing remained among people of them except their reports, they were made into reports, so He said: ﴿And We made them into tales﴾, meaning accounts whereby one converses and at which one wonders, so that they might be an admonition to those who seek insight, that they may know that the disbelievers do not prosper and the believers are not disappointed. How fine is the saying of the poet:

"Nothing endures, so be a fine tale of good remembrance, for the world is but a tale."

Since their denial brought about their destruction, which required their distance (from mercy), He said: ﴿So away with a people﴾, meaning people powerful in what is demanded of them, ﴿who do not believe﴾, meaning faith does not renew itself in them, even if the four seasons pass over them, because they have no balanced temperament.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 23, verse 45:

When the family of Pharaoh had denied belief to a human being like themselves, as those mentioned earlier, the people of Noah and the generation after them, had said, and they were the most affluent people of their time, the greatest in strength, and the most numerous in their forces, and they were enslaving the Children of Israel, and what had been transmitted to us of the signs which their Messenger showed was such that the like of it had not been transmitted to us for those who preceded him, He (glory be to Him) explicitly named them. It was as if the sending of the Message to them came after a long interval, so He indicated this with the particle of delay (ḥarf al-tarākhī, the particle indicating a lapse of time) and said: ﴿Then We sent﴾, that is, with what We possess (p-145) of greatness, ﴿Moses﴾. He increased the consolation with His saying: ﴿and his brother Aaron﴾, that is, as a supporter for him and an elucidation, because the destruction of Pharaoh and his family all together, along with the rescue of the two Messengers together and those who believed in them, is by the will of the One, the Subduer, for the success of the believers and the failure of the disbelievers. ﴿with Our signs﴾, that is, the miracles, by Our greatness, against whoever would contend with them, ﴿and a clear authority﴾, that is, a great, binding, evident proof. It is his protection, and He alone is its guardian, and its elevation over everyone who opposed him, though they, with their strength, filled the earth, and were incapable of everything they intended against him by way of plotting. And these, although they are among the signs, are the greatest of them, and they alone are sufficient to make belief obligatory.

﴿To Fir'awn (Pharaoh) and his chiefs﴾, i.e., his people.

Since the lowly do not oppose the nobles, He counted them as nonexistent. It is clear that the implied meaning is: "that you worship Allah; you have no god other than Him." By His saying ﴿but they waxed proud﴾, He indicated that they produced arrogance toward following what they were called to, immediately after the message was delivered, without reflection or deliberation. They sought not to be under the command of the one who called them. By His saying "they were," He indicated the corruption of their nature, so He said ﴿and they were a people﴾, i.e., powerful, ﴿exalted﴾ over all who opposed them among their peers.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 23, verse 47:

(p-146) When their arrogance and haughtiness gave rise to their denial of following them, He said: ﴿So they said, "Shall we believe"﴾, i.e., in God, affirming them, ﴿"to two men"﴾. Since "mithl" (like) and "ghayr" (other than) may be applied to a description of the masculine, the feminine, the dual and the plural without change, and there was no need to make it dual, He said: ﴿"like us"﴾, i.e., in humanity, in eating and drinking, and in the other things that befall human beings, just as those before them had said. ﴿"And their people"﴾, i.e., while their people ﴿"are our worshippers"﴾, i.e., in utmost humiliation and submission like slaves; so we are superior to them by this. Alas, what is wrong with them? When they made this a pretext, they did not make their inability to destroy the Messengers, and to match what they bring of miracles, a distinguishing criterion. And what is their answer to the fact that among people there is the ignorant one who cannot guide himself to anything, and the knowledgeable one who surpasses description, and that someone has made a distinction between them? And if difference between them is permissible in that respect, why is it not permissible in other respects?

So when this denial was followed by rejection, destruction followed as a consequence. He said: ﴿So they denied the two of them﴾, that is, Pharaoh and his chiefs denied Musa and Harun, upon them be peace. ﴿So they were﴾, that is, Pharaoh and his people, and by using the passive form He pointed to the immensity of His power, saying: ﴿among those who were destroyed﴾, by Our drowning them for their denial. This is an indication that they did not perish by their own doing, without a chosen destroyer, as evidenced by their all being drowned together, by the very thing that was the cause of the deliverance of all of the Children of Israel. Their strength in themselves did not avail them, nor did their strength over the Children of Israel in particular, through enslaving them, and the Children of Israel were not harmed by their weakness in defending themselves, nor by their humiliation and abasement in their hands.

And since the misguidance of their people, whom We rescued from the enslavement of Pharaoh and his people, was so astonishing, and since the listener was eager to learn what befell them after their victory, he mentioned this, opening it with the particle of expectation (*qad*), which points to their state in their misguidance, as consolation for the Prophet (ﷺ). He said: ﴿And We certainly gave﴾, that is, by Our majesty, ﴿Moses the Book﴾, that is, the one that organizes the interests of the first life and also of the second.

Since their Book was not sent down until after the destruction of Pharaoh, as is clear to anyone who considers the scattered parts of their story in the Qur'an, and since the manner of the Copts' destruction made known that the Book was for the Children of Israel, He confined Himself to their pronoun and said: ﴿so that they may be guided﴾, that is, the people of Moses and Aaron, peace be upon them both, ﴿may be guided﴾, that is, so that their condition, in the eyes of one who does not know the outcomes, would be that of those whose guidance is hoped for. The use of the expression of hope regarding them implies that among them there were those who were not guided. Ibn Kathir said: "After He sent down the Torah, no nation was destroyed in its entirety; rather, He commanded the believers to fight the disbelievers." End of quote.

It is not far from this that the pronoun in "*la'allahum*" (so that they) refers to the generations that came after, indicated by His saying ﴿generations﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 42]. Perhaps His saying, exalted is He, points to this: ﴿And We certainly gave Moses the Book after We had destroyed the former generations, as insights for people, and guidance and mercy, so that they may remember﴾ [al-Qasas: 43]. He concluded the general destruction with drowning just as He opened it with drowning. The two prophets to whom these events happened each prayed against those who disobeyed him. The Prophet (ﷺ) likened each of them, in the Battle of Badr, in severity toward the disobedient, to ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him), whom the Nile obeyed and whose army the Dajla (Tigris) obeyed.

**Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 23, verse 50:**

Since all of those mentioned had rejected those who came to them, indicating their finding it unlikely that the messengers would be human, and since the Children of Israel, whom God had honored, helped against their enemy, and clarified the path for them through the Book, had taken Jesus, despite his being a human, as a god, He followed this with mention of him, marveling at the state of the deniers in this ascent after the descent concerning the matter of those to whom they were sent, and through whose hands signs occurred for their guidance. So He said: ﴿And We made﴾, that is, by Our greatness, ﴿the son of Mary﴾, attributing him to her to confirm that he had no father, and that he was human, carried in the womb and born, and so not fit for the rank of divinity. He added to the reality of this by His saying: ﴿and his mother﴾, and He said: ﴿a sign﴾, indicating that extraordinary events appeared through the hands of both of them, to the extent that they were themselves the very sign, so that nothing of them is seen except that it is a sign. Had He said "two signs," one might have thought that the literal number was intended. Perhaps in this there is an indication that through him the sign of the power to create a human was completed in every respect: without male or female, like Adam, peace be upon him; from a male without a female, like Eve, peace be upon her; from a female without a male, like Jesus, peace be upon him; and from both spouses, like the rest of mankind. The meaning is that the Children of Israel, with the Book, which is an audible sign, and the Prophet, who is a visible sign, did not, most of them, become guided.

Since the extremists regarding Jesus and his mother, peace be upon them both, might have clung to something from this expression, He affirmed their humanity and their need, which contradicts the rank of divinity, and so He said: ﴿And We sheltered them﴾, that is, by Our greatness, when the kings of the Syrian lands intended to destroy them, ﴿on a height﴾, that is, an elevated place of the earth. The best place for vegetation is elevated ground. The apparent meaning is that it refers to ʿAyn Shams in the land of Egypt. Ibn Kathir said: ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Zayd ibn Aslam said: "There are no heights except in Egypt, and when the water is released, the villages are upon them, and were it not for the heights, the villages would be drowned."
