When deceivers in the world wanted their lie to pass, and someone to whom they had given a report hesitated over their account, they would say: "Ask so-and-so," seeking to gain trust in their report and to conceal their faults. They continued in this, persisting in ignorance of the All-Knowing, the All-Powerful, in their saying: ﴿Ask those who count﴾. That is, so that you may know the truth of our report, or because of our uncertainty about the reality of the situation, in order to establish the true length of the term. It is also possible that they intended to soften the matter toward themselves, by indicating that what they were suffering of torment preoccupied them from imagining something present and perceptible, let alone something past, let alone something reflected upon. How much more so if it were a reckoning.

This is the commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 23, verse 114:

When that was the case, on the assumption that the admission would not benefit them, because the recompense for them is punishment, given their resolve to persist in obstinacy throughout the ages, and given that the one among them who affirms it is immersed in corruption, He granted their request regarding their count, in an expression that is fitting and truthful, concerning the length of their stay, whether it was long or short. He did this by His saying, in the form of a resumptive statement (istinaf) for whoever is eager to know their answer: ﴿He said﴾. That is, God, according to the reading of the majority. The reading of Hamzah and al-Kisa'i (ʿAsim's reading not included) makes clear that attributing the saying to Him, glorified is He, is a metaphor for the saying of one of His great servants. So he said, in the first reading: ﴿Say﴾, that is, to these people from whom turning away has occurred: ﴿If﴾, that is, ﴿you did not remain﴾, that is, in the world, (p-195) ﴿except a little﴾, that is, it is so little that it is not counted, rather it is nothing: ﴿had you known﴾, that is, as a state that is like innate nature, ﴿you knew﴾, that is, among those who know at that time, you would have preferred the perishable over the enduring, and you would have turned to what benefits you, and you would have abandoned the debauchery that no rational person approves of. Engaging in it, even on the assumption of being content with it, would only happen after finishing what is important. But you were among the cattle. In this there is an admonition to the believers, who are the inheritors, to be thankful for what He granted them of joy at the destruction of their enemies and the inheritance of their land and their homes, together with their honor and blessing in their lifespans, after relieving them of those enemies in the world, and then by the continuation of their happiness in the Hereafter and the wretchedness of their enemies.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (*Nazm al-Durar*) on surah 23, verse 115:

Since their state, in their assumption that there would be no resurrection, was such that they were occupied with joy, exultation and mockery, and with ridiculing the people of Allah, they were in the condition of one who thinks that the King, the Real, the Manifest, acts in vain. Therefore, as a coordination (*ʿaṭf*) with His saying ﴿you took them as objects of ridicule﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 110], He made the consequence of that a denunciation of them in His saying: ﴿Did you think﴾. It is also permissible that it be coordinated with an implied element (*muqaddar*) such as: "Did you think that We would leave you neglected, and not do justice to your oppressed from your oppressors? So you thought ﴿that We created you﴾," that is, in accordance with the greatness that is ours, ﴿in vain﴾, that is, as those who act in vain, or for vanity from Us or from you, not for the wisdom of manifesting justice and grace, so that you would be occupied with wronging yourselves and others. Abu Hayyan said: "Vanity (*ʿabath*) is the empty kernel that has no benefit."

﴿And that you﴾, that is, and you thought that you, ﴿to Us﴾, that is, exclusively, ﴿would not be returned﴾ in any way whatsoever, in order to manifest power and greatness in the decisive judgment. Ibn Abi Hatim in his *Tafsir*, Abu Yaʿla al-Mawsili in the twenty-fourth part of his *Musnad*, and al-Baghawi in his *Tafsir* related from Ibn Mas'ud (may Allah be pleased with him) that he performed ruqyah (recitation for healing) upon a man afflicted by this verse, up to the end of the surah, into his ears, and he was healed. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "By Him in whose hand is my soul! If a man with certain faith recited it upon a mountain, it would have moved." In the chain (*sanad*) of both of them is Ibn Lahiʿah.

Ibn Kathir said: Abu Nuʿaym related from Muhammad ibn Ibrahim ibn al-Harith, from his father (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent us on a military expedition (*sariyyah*) and commanded us to say, when we entered the evening and the morning, ﴿Did you think﴾ – the verse." He said: "We recited it, and we gained booty and were safe."

Since the implied meaning was: "The matter is not as you supposed," he gave the reason for that by saying: ﴿Exalted is Allah﴾, i.e., He is high, the One who possesses majesty and beauty, exalted to a great height above futility (ʿabath). Then he described Him with what contradicts futility, saying: ﴿the King﴾, i.e., the One who encompasses the people of His kingdom in knowledge, power, governance, protection, and care.

Since some kings of this world may do what contradicts the character of kings, such as futility, with what it contains of falsehood, he followed that with an attribute that declares Him free of it, saying: ﴿the Truth﴾, i.e., the One to whom falsehood has no access in anything of His essence or attributes. So there is no ceasing for Him or for His kingdom, and how could futility reach Him?

Since the Truth as such may have a second, he negated that regarding Him, exalted is He, saying: ﴿There is no god but He﴾. So there is no equal to Him at all, in essence or attribute. Whoever is like this possesses all the qualities of perfection and the characteristics of majesty and beauty, exalted above marks of deficiency. Futility is among the lowest attributes of deficiency, because it is devoid of wisdom, which is the foundation of perfection. Then he increased in specification and emphasis on His singularity by describing Him with an attribute that no other claims, saying: ﴿Lord of the Throne﴾, i.e., the seat (ʿarsh) that encompasses all creatures, high above them with a height nothing approaches. Then he described the Throne as ﴿the Noble﴾, because it is in the context of judging with justice and being free of futility, unlike the context of Surat al-Bara'a and Surat al-Naml, where it is for subjugation and dominance. The one described as noble is the One from whom the good things received by the servants descend, together with the nobility of His essence and His rank, and the most eloquent praise of its possessor. The noble (karim) is one who conceals the blameworthy qualities of character by displaying its excellent qualities and is free from every baseness. Al-Qazzaz said: The root of karam in the language is excellence and elevation.

(p-197)

[p. 198] Since the sense is: "So whoever calls upon Allah alone, those are the successful, the inheritors in both abodes," He connected to it His saying: ﴿And whoever calls upon another god along with Allah﴾, that is, along with the King to whom none is equal, because He encompasses all the attributes of perfection, ﴿a god﴾. Since they, out of obstinacy, ascribed to the one who calls upon Him, glory be to Him, two or more names, attributing them to polytheism, He restricted it with His saying: ﴿other﴾. Then He awakened them from the slumber of heedlessness and drew attention to striving and reflection during the period of respite, with a statement more just than which there is none and more equitable, so He said: ﴿for which he has no proof﴾. Since what is intended is anything that is called a proof, even on the least of the sufficient grounds, He used the preposition **بِـ** (bi, "with/by") rather than **عَلى** (ʿalā, "upon"), which implies elevation, in pursuit of the utmost equity and in preference to the clarity of proof. So He said: ﴿for which he has no proof **with it**﴾, that is, by reason of his calling. For whoever strives to establish a proof for that will find none; rather, he will find all proofs standing against the negation of that, calling to success through belief in tawhid and righteousness. This is what is meant, not that a proof might be established for something other than this. ﴿Then his reckoning is only﴾, that is, his recompense, which cannot be increased or decreased, ﴿with his Lord﴾, the One who nurtured him, and no one else nurtured him, who overwhelmed him with goodness, and no one else showed him goodness, who is more knowing of his inner and outer state than he himself is, so nothing about his affair is hidden from Him.

Since the statement that his reckoning is with this Benefactor implies one of two outcomes, either pardon through the continuation of goodness, or loss through the cause of disbelief, He said, as an answer to one who asks about this: ﴿Indeed, the disbelievers will not succeed﴾. He placed ﴿the disbelievers﴾ in the place of the pronoun, to draw attention to their disbelief and to generalize the ruling. Thus the beginning and end of the surah [p. 199] convey that success is exclusive to the believers.

Since this was so, Allah, glorified is He, commanded His Prophet ﷺ to strive earnestly in rescuing His servants, even to the point of supplicating to Allah for their reform, so that the conclusion would be with mercy for the believers, just as the opening was with their success. He said, connecting it to His saying ﴿Repel evil with that which is better﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 96], for there is no goodness better than forgiveness. Or it is connected to the meaning of ﴿He said, "How long did you remain?"﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 112], which is made clear by the reading of Ibn Kathir, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i with the imperative: ﴿And say﴾. Or the implied meaning is: "So devote worship to Him, ﴿and say﴾," because no one can estimate Him at His true worth: ﴿My Lord﴾, O You who are good to me, ﴿forgive and have mercy﴾, that is, increase in attributing these two qualities to my community, for their multiplicity, since in that is honour for me and for them. ﴿You are the best of the forgivers﴾ and ﴿You are the best of the merciful.﴾ So by His mercy they succeeded through what He enables them to do of complying with what I pointed to at the beginning of the surah. Thus he was among the believers, and among the heirs who inherit the Paradise of Firdaws, ﴿therein they will abide forever.﴾ Thus this last part corresponds to the first, with the success of every believer and the disappointment of every disbeliever. We ask Allah, exalted is He, to make us among the most merciful of the merciful and the best of the forgivers. Indeed He is the One who takes charge of hidden things and the One hoped for to reform hearts. Amen.
